draft.title: The spoken point of view
card: A spoken point of view is your own reasoned view on an issue, presented aloud to an audience. It needs a clear position and strong reasons, not just opinion.
Structure helps listeners follow. Open with a clear contention, give your main arguments in order, and end by restating your view.
Listeners cannot reread, so speakers signpost and repeat. Phrases such as "my first point" and "to sum up" guide the audience.
Techniques should suit the audience. A rhetorical question, a short story or a direct address such as "you" can engage listeners, and tone should match the occasion.
draft.remember: A spoken view needs a clear contention, ordered arguments and techniques that suit the listeners.

a.q: Why do speakers use signposting phrases such as "my second point is"?
opts: Listeners cannot reread, so they help listeners follow along
They replace the need for evidence in an argument
They make the speech sound more emotional
They show the speaker has changed their view
a.why: A listener hears a speech once, so signposts mark where the argument is going. They do not replace evidence, which is still needed to support each point.
a.clue: Think about what a listener cannot do that a reader can.

b.q: Tariq speaks to his Year 7 assembly about banning phones at lunch. He starts with a short story about a lonely lunchtime. Why is this a good choice for this audience?
opts: A short story holds young listeners and leads into his view
It proves his contention with statistics
It lets him skip his main arguments
It shows he is unsure about his position
b.why: A brief story catches the attention of a young audience and leads into the issue. It does not prove the contention by itself, so he still needs arguments afterwards.
b.clue: Think about who is listening and what holds their attention.

a.best: Listeners cannot reread, so they help listeners follow along

b.best: A short story holds young listeners and leads into his view

proposal.title: The spoken point of view
card: A spoken point of view is your own reasoned view on an issue, presented aloud to an audience. It needs a clear position and strong reasons, not just opinion.
Structure helps listeners follow. Open with a clear contention, give your main arguments in order, and end by restating your view.
Listeners hear a speech only once, so speakers signpost and repeat on purpose. Signposts such as "my first point" and "to sum up" show where the argument is up to.
Techniques should suit the audience and occasion. Young listeners tend to respond to short stories, questions and plain words, while experts may expect detailed figures.
proposal.remember: Speak to be heard once: a clear contention, ordered and signposted arguments, and techniques chosen for the listeners.

a.q: A speaker says "My second reason is" and later "So, to sum up". What do these phrases mainly do?
opts: Show listeners where the speaker is up to in the argument
Give extra evidence to support the speaker's contention
Stir strong feelings in the audience about the issue
Add variety so the speech does not sound repetitive
a.why: These phrases are signposts. A speech is heard only once, so they show listeners where the argument is up to. They are not evidence, and speakers repeat on purpose rather than trying to avoid it.
a.clue: What can a reader do that a listener cannot?

b.q: Tariq is speaking to a Year 7 assembly in favour of banning phones at lunch. Which opening best suits this audience?
opts: A short story about a student who eats lunch alone
A long list of figures from studies on phone bans
A formal definition of each type of mobile device
A detailed summary of the school's phone policy rules
b.why: A short, vivid story suits young listeners and leads into his view. The list of figures is tempting because evidence matters, but detailed figures suit an expert audience and can lose a Year 7 crowd at the start.
b.clue: Match the technique to the age of the listeners.
